caption:
Meta is handing more of its content moderation to AI, and people inside the company say it is not going well.
Insiders told the Guardian the shift has been "really a mess": smaller teams, posts removed by mistake and fewer ways to get a fix.
Meta says its AI makes 13 percent fewer mistakes than human reviewers.

paragraphs.text: Employees at Meta say the company's push to hand content moderation to artificial intelligence has gone badly. Insiders told the Guardian, in reporting published on November 25, 2026, that the shift has been "really a mess," according to a Futurism summary of that reporting published on November 27.

The staff members described AI systems that often miss nuance and remove content that should stay up. They also said the systems struggle with languages other than English, and that users who are hit by a wrong decision now have a harder time getting it reversed, Futurism reported.

According to the employees, the people who remain work on skeleton teams. Some teams have half or two thirds of the staff they used to have, and one insider said that when they tried to contact certain teams they found those teams had been disbanded entirely. One employee said that cutting human reviewers removes the people who are essential for nuanced policy decisions, and that mistakes will follow.

Another employee said that even people with a contact inside Meta now find it very difficult to reach someone who can actually help, and that the process has become much harder than before, according to Futurism.
How far the shift has gone

Meta announced in March that it would roll out more advanced AI systems for enforcing its content rules. By June, large language models had replaced human reviewers for about half of review requests, and Meta was aiming for 90 percent automation or more in some violation categories by the end of 2026, Fortune reported, citing the Financial Times.

The Decoder reported in June that the move was expected to save the company billions of dollars a year, according to the Financial Times, and that it had already led to job losses, especially among outside contractors. Employees warned at the time that the rollout was moving too fast with too little oversight.

The complaints follow several high profile errors this fall. Fortune reported on November 3 that Meta blamed mistakes in its automated systems after the Instagram account of the No Kings protest coalition was suspended on October 17 and after a Spanish language campaign account of Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon was taken down on October 27. Both accounts were later restored.

Meta rejected the claim that its moderation is dysfunctional. In a statement quoted by Futurism, the company said it has long used AI to help enforce its community standards and began testing more advanced AI systems earlier this year. Meta said its latest tests show those systems make 13 percent fewer mistakes than humans when acting on violating content and find 10 percent more actual violations. It also said users can appeal decisions. Those figures come from Meta and have not been independently verified.

The dispute comes down to which numbers matter. Meta measures accuracy on its own test sets, while the employees describe what happens when a mistake does slip through: fewer people left to catch it and fewer routes for a user to get it fixed. A system can make fewer errors on average and still leave the people it gets wrong with nowhere to turn.

The next signal is whether Meta publishes appeal and reversal rates for decisions made by its AI systems as automation passes 90 percent in some categories, which would show how often the machines are overruled.
